say: You give it a list of numbers. It finds the three values that cut the list into four equal parts, $Q_1$, $Q_2$ and $Q_3$, and the **interquartile range**.
Put the list in order first. The median splits it in half, then $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are the medians of the two halves.

how.higher: It is a step inside a bigger statistics question on Paper 2, usually worth part of a 30-mark question.
how.ordinary: It turns up as its own part on Paper 2, often 10 marks, and as a step in longer data questions, mostly Question 7 and Question 1.

example.question:
The number of text messages Aoife sent on eight days was:
$11, 4, 18, 7, 20, 13, 8, 15$
Find the interquartile range.

steps.title: Put in order, find median
steps.say: Write the numbers in order, smallest first. With eight numbers the median sits between the 4th and 5th, so it splits the list into two halves of four.

steps.title: Find the lower quartile
steps.say: $\hl{1}{Q_1}$ is the median of the lower half. Four numbers, so take the middle two and find their mean.

steps.title: Find the upper quartile
steps.say: $\hl{2}{Q_3}$ is the median of the upper half. Same method on $13, 15, 18, 20$.

higher.tip: A correct answer with no work can still earn full marks, but show the steps anyway: if one slip happens, the working is what earns partial credit.
Mark the quartiles on the diagram or list. Work done there can earn marks.

ordinary.tip: Write the data in order before anything else. Ordering the list earns marks of its own.
Finding the median from the list as given, unordered, earns little.

sources.quote: Median taken from an unordered list

ordinary.tip: Show how you get $Q_1$ before you subtract. Work towards $Q_1$ earns partial credit.

say: You give it a scatter plot. It tells you the **direction** and the **strength** of the link between the two variables, and which value of $r$ fits.
$r$ always lies between $-1$ and $1$. The sign is the direction. The closer to $1$ or $-1$, the tighter the points lie on a straight line.

how.higher: It appears as a step in Paper 2 statistics questions, such as describing a trend, drawing a line of best fit, or giving $r$ on the calculator.
how.ordinary: It is a regular part of Paper 2, most years: match $r$ to a plot, describe the relationship in words, or say what a given $r$ tells you.

example.question:
A teacher records hours of TV watched, $x$, and test score, $y$, for five students.
$x$: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
$y$: 9, 7, 6, 3, 2
The points lie close to a straight line sloping downhill. Choose the value of $r$ from $0.99$, $-0.2$, $-0.99$ and explain your choice.

steps.title: Read the direction
steps.say: Look at which way the points run. As $x$ goes up, $y$ goes down, so the **direction** is negative. That rules out $0.99$.

steps.title: Read the strength
steps.say: Look at how tight the points are. They lie close to one straight line, so the link is **strong**. A value near $0$, like $-0.2$, means a loose cloud.

lines.text: Close to a line: strong, so $r$ is near $-1$

steps.title: Choose r and explain
steps.say: Strong and negative means $r$ is close to $-1$. Give the value, then say it in words.

lines.text: Strong negative linear correlation: as TV time goes up, test score goes down.

higher.tip: Label every point you plot. Correct points with no or wrong labels lose a mark.

sources.quote: no or incorrect labels on points

higher.tip: When asked about a point far outside the data, say it is beyond the data, so the line is unreliable there.

sources.quote: L is well beyond all of the given data

ordinary.tip: Give both words: direction and strength. For example, strong and negative.
Say what the points look like: they lie close to a line, and which way it slopes.

sources.quote: Points all lie close to a positive

ordinary.tip: Put the link back into the context of the question, in plain words.

sources.quote: Cars with greater engine size are less fuel

say: You give it a data set. It finds any value that sits far away from the rest, an **outlier**.
Build a fence on each side of the middle half of the data. Anything beyond a fence is an outlier.

example.question:
Find any outliers in this data set, using the rule that an outlier lies more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ above $Q_3$ or below $Q_1$.
$3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 30$

steps.title: Find the quartiles
steps.say: The data is already in order. Find $\hl{1}{Q_1}$ and $\hl{2}{Q_3}$, the medians of the lower and upper halves.

steps.title: Find the IQR
steps.say: Subtract the quartiles to get the width of the middle half.

steps.title: Build the fences
steps.say: Go $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ beyond each quartile. Beyond these, a value is an outlier.

steps.title: Compare each value
steps.say: Check the smallest and largest values against the fences. Only $30$ is outside.

say: You give it a frequency table with the data in groups. It estimates the **mean**, because you no longer know the exact values.
Pretend every value in a group sits at the middle of that group, the **mid-interval value**. Then find the mean the usual way.

how.higher: It is a step in a longer Paper 2 statistics question, for example forming an equation in an unknown frequency from a given mean.
how.ordinary: It appears as a part of its own on Paper 2, worth about 5 marks, or as a step in a longer question on a frequency table.

example.question:
The table shows the number of minutes 20 students spent on homework.
Minutes: 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40
Number of students: 3, 7, 6, 4
Estimate the mean time.

steps.title: Find mid-interval values
steps.say: Take the middle of each group. Add the two ends and halve.

steps.title: Multiply by frequency
steps.say: Multiply each mid-value $\hl{1}{x}$ by the number of students $f$, then add them up.

steps.title: Divide by total frequency
steps.say: Add the frequencies to get the number of students, then divide.

higher.tip: Start by finding the mid-interval values. It is the first step the marks are tied to.
With an unknown frequency, put it in both the top and the bottom of the mean, then write an equation.

ordinary.tip: Show each mid-value times its frequency, added together, before you divide.
The question tells you to use mid-interval values. Do it: using the group ends loses the marks.
